statement: (i) Use the substitution $x=\sin\theta$ to evaluate $\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,dx$. (ii) Hence state the area bounded by $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ and the x-axis. (iii) Show that $\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
solution: (i) $x=\sin\theta$, $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$, $\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\cos\theta$; limits $0\to\pi/2$. Integral $=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$. (ii) This is exactly that area, a quarter of the unit circle: $\frac{\pi}{4}$. (iii) $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}=\arcsin x$, so $[0,1]=\arcsin 1-\arcsin 0=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
hints: Substitute x=sin theta and change limits.
